The Common cuckoo Cuculus canorus is an obligate brood parasite whose life history is shaped by its unique reproductive strategy. Measurements taken from field studies indicate that newly hatched chicks weigh a mere 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of altricial cuckoo offspring. Under the thermal regime typical of active adult metabolism, which stabilizes around 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the period from hatching to fledging, or the age at which a young cuckoo is capable of sustained flight, is a tightly constrained developmental window. Field observations have consistently documented that fledging occurs 19 days after birth [tx = 19 days after birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This rapid developmental phase allows the juvenile cuckoo to vacate the host nest quickly, reducing the risk of predation and detection by the host parents.

At the elevated body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], several key reproductive and developmental milestones are calibrated. Sexual maturity, signaled by the completion of gametogenesis and the onset of gonadal activity, is reached relatively early in this species. Captive-reared Common cuckoos attain puberty at 57 days after birth [tp = 57 days after birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively short interval to reproductive competence is somewhat unusual for a bird of this body mass, but it aligns with the species' need to exploit a broad temporal window for parasitizing a diverse array of host nests. The first successful breeding event, or the laying of a cuckoo egg in a suitable host nest, typically occurs later in the life cycle. The most reliable field estimates suggest that females initiate their first brood at 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth], meaning first reproduction is deferred until the second calendar year of life at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].

The ultimate adult body size and mass of the Common cuckoo are well characterized from extensive museum specimen series and field measurements. Adult individuals, irrespective of sex, reach a maximum longitudinal extent or total length of 33 centimeters [Li = 33 centimeters], a dimension that includes the bird's elongated tail feathers crucial for its concealment during egg-laying. Correspondingly, the mature body mass, or ultimate wet weight attained by an adult cuckoo in the wild, is approximately 115 grams [Wwi = approximately 115 grams]. This mass is relatively modest for a species within the Cuculiformes, reflecting a body plan optimized for agile flight and stealth rather than for carrying large bodily reserves. The lifespan of the Common cuckoo, derived from long-term ringing and recapture programs, has provided insights into its maximum longevity. At the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the oldest documented free-living individual lived for 4709 days [am = 4709 days], which translates to nearly 13 years.

Reproductive output in the Common cuckoo is not expressed as a simple daily rate but rather through discrete reproductive events that depend on host availability and egg-laying capacity. During the breeding season, a female cuckoo typically lays a single egg per nesting attempt in each parasitized host nest [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt in each parasitized host nest]. Over the course of the entire breeding season, which spans several months, a highly productive female may achieve a maximum frequency of approximately 9 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 9 clutches per year]. When this high clutch frequency is combined with the consistent single-egg clutch size, it yields a formidable annual fecundity. This maximum laying rate is physiologically demanding, requiring precise timing and the rapid mobilization of calcium for eggshell production, and it is only achieved under optimal foraging conditions and host availability. The data underscore the cuckoo's evolutionary refinement as a reproductive specialist.

The incubation and hatching dynamics of the Common cuckoo are profoundly influenced by the thermal environment of the host's nest, rather than by the cuckoo's own body temperature. The age at hatching, or the incubation period from egg deposition to the emergence of the neonate, is primarily determined by the temperature maintained by the host parent. Controlled laboratory experiments using artificial incubation, designed to mimic host nest conditions, have shown that at a constant temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the cuckoo embryo develops and hatches in 11.65 days [ab = 11.65 days]. This remarkably short incubation period is a key adaptation of the brood parasitic strategy, as it allows the cuckoo chick to hatch before the host's own offspring, giving it a critical competitive advantage in securing food and parental care. The 11.65 day incubation period is among the shortest recorded for any bird of comparable egg size, highlighting a life history trade-off between rapid embryonic development and the initial energetic reserves available to the hatchling. The birth mass of 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams] is among the smallest for any cuckoo species.
